title: Short Stuff: ZIP Codes!
summary: Short Stuff episode on ZIP codes. The hosts trace postal codes to a London district system in 1857, and explain that US ZIP codes arrived July 1, 1963 to speed mail sorting as cities grew. They credit postal inspector Robert Moon of Philadelphia with the concept (joking that the USPS took his idea), explain that ZIP stands for Zone Improvement Plan and that the trademark lapsed, and describe the structure of the five-digit code: the first digit is the national area, the next two the sectional center, and the last two the post office. They cover the ZIP+4 system from 1983, buildings and places with their own ZIP codes (White House, Empire State Building, Burning Man, Houston Astrodome after Katrina), towns that lost codes (Centralia, Pennsylvania, in 1992), Santa Claus's ZIP code 99701, and the wealthiest ZIP codes (Alpine, New Jersey, and Fisher Island, Florida).

segments.title: Introduction and ZIP code origins in London
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode with Zippy (Mister Zip) and begin with the 1857 London postal district system as a precursor to ZIP codes.

segments.title: Why ZIP codes were created
segments.summary: Zip codes arose from growing urban density and the need to speed mail delivery. The US adopted them on July 1, 1963, and there are 41,642 today.

segments.title: Robert Moon and the origin of the ZIP concept
segments.summary: Philadelphia postal inspector Robert Moon is credited with the ZIP concept, which the USPS adopted. ZIP stands for Zone Improvement Plan, and the trademark was allowed to expire.

segments.title: Pre-ZIP mail routing and early adoption
segments.summary: Before ZIP codes, mail passed through many sorting stops. The codes narrowed routing at each stop. The PR and marketing push included Mister Zip and an Ethel Merman commercial.

segments.title: Mid-episode teaser and break
segments.summary: Brief banter and a lead-in to the break before the explanation of the number structure.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Sponsor read and a break in the episode.

segments.title: Decoding the five-digit ZIP code
segments.summary: The first digit is the national area, from 0 in the northeast to 9 on the West Coast, Hawaii and Alaska. The next two digits identify the sectional center, which may be a large city, and the last two identify the post office.

segments.title: ZIP+4 and buildings with their own ZIP codes
segments.summary: The ZIP+4 system from 1983 narrows delivery to a block side or building floor. The White House has two ZIP codes, and the Empire State Building, World Trade Center and Burning Man also have their own.

segments.title: Temporary and revoked ZIP codes
segments.summary: After Hurricane Katrina, the Houston Astrodome received a temporary ZIP code. Centralia, Pennsylvania lost its ZIP code in 1992 because of a mine fire.

segments.title: Santa Claus ZIP code and wealthiest ZIP codes
segments.summary: Santa Claus was given ZIP code 99701. Canada's Santa code is H0H 0H0. The hosts look up the wealthiest ZIP codes, Alpine, New Jersey and Fisher Island, Florida, and note Beverly Hills is not the wealthiest.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts close the Short Stuff episode and give the iHeartRadio credit.
